extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, PTO/IPR practitioners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical standards for evaluating obviousness challenges and secondary-consideration evidence in inter partes review (IPR) proceedings and for assessing whether the PTAB properly considered late-raised reply arguments. Focuses on nexus, presumption of nexus, Graham factors, substantial-evidence review, and reply-brief limits under 37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claimed invention to be patentable, the differences between it and the prior art must be such that a relevant artisan at the priority date would not have found the claimed subject matter as a whole obvious. Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying facts including the scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, the level of ordinary skill, and relevant evidence of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Graham v. John Deere and KSR: consider (1) scope and content of prior art, (2) differences between prior art and claims, (3) level of ordinary skill, and (4) secondary considerations. Court reviews legal determinations de novo and factual findings for substantial-evidence support. (See Henny Penny; KSR; Graham.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia of nonobviousness include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved need, industry praise, competitor licenses, and failure of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence must have a 'legally and factually sufficient connection' (nexus) to the claimed invention to be relevant. If nexus exists and the product is coextensive with the claims, a presumption of nexus may apply. The Board may give substantial weight to secondary considerations if nexus is established. (Cites: Graham; Fox Factory; Brown & Williamson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of nexus from a coextensive marketed product
rubrics_metrics.description: A nexus between secondary-consideration evidence and the claimed invention is presumed when 'the marketed product embodies the claimed features, and is coextensive with them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coextensiveness inquiry compares only the claim with the commercial product and can give rise to a presumption of nexus (Immunex quoting WBIP). However, the presumption does not decide the final nexus question when the connection between the commercial product and the prior art undermines nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus lacking when evidence relates exclusively to feature known in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness lacks a nexus if it exclusively relates to a feature that was 'known in the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the feature responsible for commercial success (or other secondary evidence) was taught by the prior art and a skilled artisan would have been motivated to use it (with a reasonable expectation of success) to make the claimed invention, then that secondary evidence is not pertinent to nonobviousness. (Cites: Rambus; Ormco; Ethicon.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus may attach to an individual element or to an inventive combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary-consideration evidence may be linked either to an individual claim element or to the inventive combination of known elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence is tied to the combination (and not to a single pre-existing feature), WBIP allows treating 'the claimed combination as a whole' as the nexus for objective evidence. But where evidence 'relate[s] entirely' to a single feature present in the prior art, the WBIP rationale for treating the combination as nexus does not save that evidence from being unhelpful to the obviousness inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial-evidence standard for factual findings; de novo for legal conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court reviews the Board’s legal determinations de novo and the Board’s factual findings for substantial-evidence support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding is supported by substantial evidence if a reasonable mind might accept the evidence as adequate to support the finding. (Cites: Henny Penny; Consolidated Edison.) Absent substantial-evidence support for a nexus or other factual finding, the Board’s ultimate legal conclusion on obviousness may be reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b) — limits on reply briefs in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: A reply may only respond to arguments raised in the corresponding opposition, patent owner preliminary response, patent owner response, or decision on institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner may not raise in reply 'an entirely new rationale' that was not in the petition or responsive to the patent owner’s response. The rule reflects efficiency and fairness, and the statutory requirement that the petition identify 'with particularity' the grounds for challenge (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)). (Cites: 37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b); Intelligent Bio-Systems; Ariosa; Apple v. Andrea.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion to decline new arguments raised in reply; abuse-of-discretion review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must judge when a reply contention crosses the line from responsive to new, and may decline to consider new arguments raised only in reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board’s decision on this matter is reviewed for abuse of discretion. The Board abuses its discretion if its decision (1) is clearly unreasonable, arbitrary, or fanciful; (2) is based on an erroneous conclusion of law; (3) rests on clearly erroneous fact finding; or (4) involves a record that contains no evidence on which the Board could rationally base its decision. (Cites: Henny Penny; Intelligent Bio-Systems.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper petition content and consequences of reserving new theories for reply
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner must present its grounds and rationales in its petition; arguments first presented in reply that are 'meaningfully distinct' from the petition may be treated as untimely new contentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petitioner could have but did not present an argument in the petition (e.g., that it would have been obvious to modify a prior-art reference to meet a claim limitation), the Board may decline to consider it when raised only in reply. The petitioner is the 'master of its complaint' and cannot rely on reply briefing to introduce new theories. (Cites: Intelligent Bio-Systems; Ariosa; Acceleration Bay; SAS Institute.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima-facie analysis at institution/decision stages and specificity for discrete claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A challenge to patentability must reason as to why prior art renders a claimed limitation obvious; absence of disclosure of a specific limitation in the asserted prior art can lead the Board to find the prima-facie case unpersuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Board finds that a claimed limitation (e.g., a 1/8-inch tolerance) is not disclosed by the asserted references, that finding can render secondary-consideration evidence immaterial for that claim subset. A petitioner must explain modifications or optimizations to prior art references in its petition rather than in a late reply. (Illustrated by the Board's handling of the one-eighth-inch limitation in the '834 patent IPR.)
